Finding Superman

Any proceeds from this first adventure are intended for donation to the Taya and Chris Kyle Foundation (Service Family Strong). All funds directed there in honor of those who serve.

The morning light in Metropolis is clear and a little sharp. I have driven far enough that the town feels like both a destination and a pause. I am looking for Superman — not the comic-book figure, but the idea of someone who might understand the weight that still rides with me. The years in uniform from 1989 to 1994. The Doha Dash. The divorce and the children I did not raise all the way to adulthood. The deliberate choice, later, to heal among wolves instead of on a range so the sights, sounds, and smells would not keep winning.

Half the stoicism people notice on me is simply fear held still. So I stay quiet and observe. Chris Kyle’s monument in Odessa remains in the back of my mind: the statue, the plaques, the signatures of his wife and kids on the bottom of his boot. Standing there I felt small, almost unworthy of handing a legend anything at all. A plaque at the memorial said something that stayed with me: when a veteran gets a hand up, he does not grab with both hands. He reaches back with one hand to help the next veteran. A brother gave me that hand up. He is the reason I came to El Paso. I have tried, in my own way, to keep one hand free. At Wolf Creek Habitat a litter arrived; I named the only male Crisou after his grandfather, a blind arctic wolf. The day he was finally ready to meet people felt like the first day of school. I was proud. Those moments, and others like them, are what keep pushing me to be better and to help other veterans who carry similar loads. I still think of the small town of Carthage, Indiana, where I grew up — the banners that later honored roughly 500 veterans from a town of about 500, including my own family and my big brother Bob.

Now the streets of Metropolis open in front of me. Somewhere in this town there is a 30-foot statue, a cage that looks emptied, playful versions of the hero, and a life-sized figure whose cape I will be allowed to hold. The search is quiet, but it is still a search.

The Cage, the Globe, and the Watchful Vehicle

Behind a chain-link fence the metal globe rises, wires and lights still clinging to its frame. A sign for the Daily Planet and the Super Museum sits low. Nearby is the cage. Something inside could pass for kryptonite; the bars are bent outward as if whatever was held there simply pushed free and left. Superman escaped. The thought lands gently. Even the strongest still have to break out of something.

A green armored sheriff vehicle rests on the pavement, solid and practical. I stand a moment and think of the veterans I hope to help — how many of us are still looking for the bent bar, the opening, the day we decide we are ready to step out and meet the world again. Crisou taught me something about that patience. I keep walking.

Riddle: What material was Superman’s greatest weakness often called?

The Fakes, the Windows, and the Playful Versions

The town enjoys its hero. A Marilyn Monroe figure wears a Superman cape dress and sits above a small chair and a Kewpie doll. A large Big Boy hybrid stands with the S shield on his chest. Supergirl is painted across windows with stars and an American flag. A Viking figure watches from Thor’s Gym. Cutouts and decals appear in shop glass. They are harmless, a little absurd, and they make me smile in spite of myself.

Not every hero has to be real. Sometimes a town just wants to remember the idea. It also reminds me that imitation is easy — people have already begun copying my look and the quiet way I carry myself — while the actual work of healing is slower and less visible. I stay quiet, observe, and keep moving down the sidewalk.

Riddle: In which Illinois town is this adventure set?

The 30-Foot Superman

At the courthouse the statue rises thirty feet against the brick building and the clear sky. The base is carved with the words “Truth – Justice – The American Way.” I stand at the bottom, look up, and remember the old song. For a private second I pretend to tug on his cape. He does not move. He does not need to. Underneath the legend he is only life-sized — a person with exceptional skills, nothing more and nothing less.

I take a selfie, pointing, still here. The Odessa monument feels both closer and farther away. There I felt small beside a legend. Here I feel the same smallness, yet I am still walking, still trying to become someone who can help others the way certain hard-won moments once helped me. The cape does not need to be tugged. The choice to keep going is enough.

Riddle: What famous song warns “you don’t tug on Superman’s cape”?

The Gift Shop and the Life-Sized Figure

Inside the gift shop the light is softer. Posters, framed photographs, and an American flag surround a life-sized Superman. The owners are kind. They let me step close and take a picture while I hold his cape — the way I once might have held something I was not sure I deserved. The flash goes off. For a moment the weight feels lighter.

I have come a long way: through service, through loss, through the wolves and Crisou, through the quiet streets of this town, through the choice to stay quiet when fear wears the face of stoicism. The hope that travels with me is simple — that some of what I have learned can be useful to other veterans who feel the same weight. For now I thank the owners, step back outside, and keep walking.

Riddle: What was the name of the wolf named after a blind arctic wolf grandfather?

Arlington, the Procession, and Two Kinds of Healing

I was in Arlington, Texas, at work when the news showed the procession. Motorcycles leading the casket of Chris Kyle. I did not know his story then. Later I learned it — what the years had asked of him, what recovery asked of him and his family, how even a legend could not simply come home and fit back in.

I did not have the same opportunity. I was not as connected to the military as I should have been. My mindset was to just keep moving forward, and that was enough until something traumatic or triggering happened. I did not know what PTSD was, and neither did anyone around me. In that way I was expected to come home and fit in, the same expectation once placed on the Vietnam veterans in Carthage. Chris Kyle could not. My big brother Bob could not. And I could not.

That is part of why the choice of wolves over weapons still matters to me. Weapon healing and wolf healing are not the same path. One can keep the triggers close; the other asks for patience, nature, and the slow work of learning to trust again — the way Crisou eventually did. This adventure is an attempt to share that difference mindfully, without anger, in the hope that another veteran might recognize the road and choose a next step of their own.

Crisou

At Wolf Creek Habitat in Brookville, Indiana, a litter of wolves arrived. I named the only male Crisou after his grandfather, a blind arctic wolf. Watching him learn to trust people felt like the first day of school. I was a proud parent that day. He became part of the reason I chose wolves over weapons — a patient, living reminder that healing can happen in nature, one careful step at a time.

The Chris Kyle Memorial

In Odessa the statue stands. I stood there and felt small — almost unworthy of handing a legend anything. The plaques, the signatures on the boot, the quiet weight of the place. A plaque reminded me that when a veteran receives a hand up, he does not grab with both hands. He reaches back with one hand to help the next. A brother gave me that hand up. He is the reason I came to El Paso. I have tried to keep one hand free.

Carthage, the Banners, and a Legend

I grew up in the small town of Carthage, Indiana. Kids were told to just leave the Vietnam veterans alone. Most of them had been drafted — farmers who came home and were expected to fit straight back into ordinary life after everything they had seen. PTSD, flashbacks, and even the pesticides sprayed on the crops could still reach them. The silence around them was its own kind of instruction.

A couple of months ago I went home for a celebration. They had made banners for all the veterans who served from Carthage. Mine was there, along with about a dozen family members — uncles, cousins, grandparents, and great-grandparents. More than anyone else. My big brother Bob, a Vietnam veteran with two Purple Hearts and a legend to me, I consider family too. They said there are about 500 veterans from a town whose population is about 500.

Standing among those banners I understood again why the quiet observation, the choice to heal in nature, and the desire to offer something other veterans can grasp all feel necessary. The Metropolis walk is part of that same long road.

A Quiet Riddle

About Chris Kyle: In which Texas city was the American Sniper born — the same city where a memorial statue now stands in his honor?

A psychologist once helped me build a simple safety plan, and a few people stayed close enough to check in while I found my footing again. Their quiet consistency gave me room to keep moving. The mind remembers hard things easily. The heart still looks for better ones. This story, and any that follow, exist because hope kept a place at the table.
